d.title: `dtype=object` means the array is not doing what you think
d.caption: **Every operation falls back to a Python-level loop over boxed objects, so the vectorisation you came for is gone and the array is a list with extra steps** — and `dtype='<U32'` is the same problem with a fixed-width string, which also silently truncates anything longer. The tell is cheap: **print the dtype, and if it is `object` on numeric data, find the `None` or the string that caused it.** And the second row is the cost nobody budgets for: **float64 to float32 halves the memory and is usually enough for features**, which matters at the scale where it matters at all.

d.title: `np.vectorize` is the trap in this list
d.caption: **It looks like the answer to “how do I vectorise this function” and it is a convenience wrapper around a Python loop — so it gives you the broadcasting *semantics* and none of the speed.** The real tools are the ones that keep the loop out of Python: **`np.where` for a conditional, boolean masks for a filter, `np.select` for several conditions, and the ufuncs for arithmetic.** And the general test: **if the expression contains a Python-level `for` or a `lambda` applied per element, the loop did not leave Python**, whatever the wrapper is called.

nodes.label: np.vectorize
nodes.sub: a wrapper around a Python loop

A boolean mask for a filter
Test: is there a per-element lambda?

d.title: `.loc` slices include the endpoint and `.iloc` slices do not
d.caption: **`df.loc[3:5]` gives three rows and `df.iloc[3:5]` gives two** — which is the one asymmetry in pandas indexing that catches everybody, and it is deliberate: a label slice has no notion of “one past the end”. The practical rule that follows: **use `.loc` for labels and `.iloc` for positions, and never bare `df[...]`**, because bare brackets mean a column on a string, a row slice on a slice, and a boolean filter on a mask — **three different operations behind one syntax.**

d.title: `memory_usage='deep'` is the only number that counts the strings
d.caption: **The default reports the pointer array and not the objects it points at, so a DataFrame of text looks far smaller than it is** — and `deep=True` follows them. Which is 10.3's `getsizeof` problem in another library. The fix for the usual culprit is one line: **an object column with few distinct values becomes a `category` and loses most of its memory**, because the strings are stored once. And the second: **downcasting int64 to int32 or float64 to float32 where the range allows it** is free in accuracy terms and halves the column.

state: half the column, no accuracy cost

d.title: `groupby` drops NaN keys by default, so the summary does not sum to the total
d.caption: **A column with missing values produces a summary that silently excludes those rows** — and the giveaway is exactly that: the group totals do not add up to the overall total, which nobody checks. **`dropna=False` includes them as their own group.** The merge equivalent is the companion bug: **a left join that unexpectedly grows the row count means the right side was not unique on the key** — so **`validate="m:1"` turns that into an exception rather than a silent duplication of every matched row.**

d.title: Six situations, and pandas is the right answer to exactly one of them
d.caption: **Under about a gigabyte and exploratory — that is where pandas is genuinely the right tool, and the row is worth stating because the rest of the table reads as a dismissal otherwise.** Two rows are about not moving the data at all: **if it is already in a database, do not fetch it to aggregate it**, and larger-than-memory wants DuckDB over Parquet. And the last is a judgement rather than a size: **in a production pipeline, pandas' looseness is a liability** — silent dtype changes and index alignment are features for exploration and hazards in a job.

d.title: `lazy=True` reports every violation at once
d.caption: **Without it you fix one column, re-run for ten minutes, and discover the next one** — so a schema check on a large file is a sequence of ten-minute round trips rather than one report. Which is the whole argument for the flag, and it generalises: **a validator that stops at the first error turns a batch problem into a serial one.** The schema's other job is the one that outlasts the data: **it is a written contract, so a column rename upstream fails here with a name rather than three transformations later with a `KeyError`.**

nodes.label: Default: stop at the first violation
So fixing ten columns takes ten runs
And the schema is a written contract
So a rename fails HERE, with a name

d.title: The rejection threshold is what separates tolerance from negligence
d.caption: **Skipping a few malformed rows is sensible; skipping a third of the file is a silent outage** — and the only difference between them is a number somebody wrote down. So the shape that works: **count the rejects, write them somewhere inspectable, and fail the run when the proportion crosses the threshold.** The part people omit is the middle one: **a reject count with no sample is a number you cannot act on**, because the fix depends on *why* they failed — and the rejects file is the only artefact that answers that.

nodes.label: Skip a third of the file
The difference is a written threshold
And fail the run above the threshold

d.title: Freshness is the check that catches the most incidents
d.caption: **A pipeline that reprocesses yesterday's file succeeds every time, reports green, and produces a stale answer** — and no row-level validation will ever notice, because every row is valid. Which is why **the max timestamp in the data is the single highest-value assertion in a data pipeline**, and it costs one query. The other three are about distribution rather than correctness: **row count against the recent average, null rate per column, and the distribution of a key numeric field** — each catching an upstream change that produces valid-looking data.

d.title: Five notebook problems with one cause and mostly one fix
d.caption: **All five come from the same thing: a notebook is JSON with embedded outputs, execution counts and metadata, so every run changes the file even when the code did not.** `nbstripout` on commit fixes four of them outright — **unreadable diffs, unresolvable conflicts, and repository bloat from a base64 PNG per plot per commit.** The fifth needs more: **an API key echoed in a cell output is committed and permanent, so stripping has to be paired with a secret scanner** — because the strip is a convention and the scanner is the enforcement.

d.title: The executed notebook as an artefact is the real argument for papermill
d.caption: **For a report a human reads, the output *is* the deliverable — so running a parameterised notebook and keeping the executed copy gives you the result and the evidence in one file**, which a script's stdout does not. Which is the narrow case where a notebook belongs in a scheduler at all. The conditions that make it safe: **parameters injected rather than edited, a pinned environment, outputs written to a dated path, and a non-zero exit on failure** — and without that last one **a failed notebook run looks exactly like a successful one.**

d.title: `fit_transform` on test data is the single most common leakage bug
d.caption: **And it looks harmless — it is one method name, on the line you would naturally write** — which is why it survives review and produces a model that scores well and fails in production. The contract is the defence: **`fit` learns parameters and `transform` applies them, so test data gets `transform` only, with the parameters learned on train.** A `Pipeline` makes it structural rather than remembered: **`fit` on the pipeline fits each step on train and `predict` transforms only**, so the correct thing is the easy thing.

nodes.label: The scaler learned the test distribution

d.title: Two of these splitters exist because a random split is a correctness bug
d.caption: **With time order, a random split trains on the future — the model sees tomorrow's data and reports a score it cannot reproduce on a single real day.** With groups, **the same customer in train and test is leakage**, because the model can memorise the customer rather than learn the behaviour. Both produce a *better* cross-validation score than the honest split, **which is what makes them dangerous rather than merely wrong.** And the last row is the honest admission: **neither alone is sufficient when you have both.**

d.title: The `__init__` rule is not stylistic
d.caption: **`clone()` reconstructs an estimator from `get_params()`, so a parameter transformed in `__init__` is lost — and `clone()` is called by every cross-validation, every grid search and every pipeline fit.** Which means the rule *“store constructor arguments unchanged, with the same names”* is what makes an estimator usable at all: **validate in `fit`, not in `__init__`, and derive nothing until then.** The symptom when it is broken is characteristic: **the estimator works alone and misbehaves inside `GridSearchCV`**, with no error.

nodes.label: Called by every CV, search and pipeline
So a transform in __init__ is lost
Symptom: fine alone, wrong in GridSearchCV

d.title: Three formats, and the one everybody uses is portable in neither sense
d.caption: **A pickled model needs the same classes and the same library versions to load, and loading it is arbitrary code execution** — which is 7.3's argument applied to the artefact a data scientist hands to a platform team. So it is fine inside one trust boundary and your own infrastructure, **and it is the wrong thing to accept from anywhere else.** ONNX is the answer for serving: **a computation graph that any runtime in any language can load safely** — which also decouples the serving stack from the training stack's versions.

d.title: `git_dirty` is the field people omit and need
d.caption: **A commit sha recorded from a working tree with uncommitted changes describes code that does not exist anywhere** — so the artefact claims reproducibility it does not have, and the discrepancy only surfaces when someone tries to rebuild it months later. Which makes the metadata set short and specific: **the commit sha, whether the tree was dirty, the data version or content hash, the library versions, and the random seed.** And the reason all five travel together: **any one of them missing makes the other four insufficient to reproduce the run.**

nodes.label: Dirty + a sha = code that does not exist
Plus data hash, library versions, seed
Any one missing makes the rest insufficient
nodes.sub: which is why they travel together

d.title: `--preload` loads the model once and shares it copy-on-write
d.caption: **Under gunicorn the model is loaded in the master and inherited by every worker, so four workers cost one model's memory rather than four** — which for anything large is the difference between fitting on the instance and not. The caveat is worth knowing before you enable it: **copy-on-write means memory is shared only while nothing writes to it**, so a model that mutates state per request de-shares its pages and you are back to four copies. And the other half: **load at import or in a lifespan hook, never on the first request**, or the first user pays for it and the health check passes before the model exists.

nodes.label: And load at import or in lifespan
Or the health check passes too early

d.title: Output drift is the cheapest signal you will ever add
d.caption: **It needs no labels, it moves within hours of an upstream change, and it is a histogram of your own predictions** — which is why it catches the failures that accuracy monitoring cannot, because accuracy needs ground truth that arrives weeks later or never. The four silent failures share one property: **the service returns 200 and a plausible number throughout.** A feature that stopped arriving becomes a default, a renamed category becomes an unknown, **and a model loaded from a stale artefact predicts confidently with last quarter's weights.**

d.title: Jitter is not optional on a rate limit
d.caption: **Without it every rate-limited client retries at the same instant, so the limiter rejects them all again and the pattern repeats** — 14.2's measurement from the NLP course arriving as an LLM concern: a synchronised retry wave is the original spike, repeated. The rest of the policy is about which failures deserve a retry at all: **a 429 and a 5xx yes, with backoff; a 400 and a context-length error never, because they will fail identically.** And the bound that matters most: **a cap on total attempts *and* on total time**, since a retried LLM call is a bill as well as a delay.

nodes.label: The limiter rejects them all again
Cap attempts AND total time
nodes.sub: a retry is a bill too

d.title: Shedding stale work is what breaks the death spiral
d.caption: **Once every queued job is older than its client's timeout, the system is spending 100% of its capacity producing results nobody will read** — and because it is still busy, the queue keeps growing. Which is the spiral, and adding capacity does not break it. **Dropping a job whose deadline has already passed is the only move that recovers**, because it converts wasted work back into throughput. The mechanism is small: **stamp each job with a deadline on arrival, and check it before starting rather than after finishing.**

nodes.label: The queue grows past the timeout
Adding capacity does not break it

d.title: Prompt caching is the highest-value option for most applications
d.caption: **Because a long stable system prompt is the largest part of the request, and ~90% off the cached prefix applies to every call rather than only to repeats.** The exact-match cache saves 100% and helps only on identical input, which in a chat application is almost never. And the semantic cache is the one to be careful with: **100% on *similar* input, at the cost of an embedding call per request and false hits** — so it is trading correctness for cost, which needs a threshold somebody chose deliberately.
